scope.functional_unit: 1 kg of brown seaweed-based bioplastic film providing barrier performance equivalent to conventional PE film for food packaging (service: protection of 1 m² of food product for 30 days at 4 °C)
scope.system_boundary: Cradle‑to‑grave for the bioplastic film, including seaweed cultivation (offshore longline), harvest, transport to shore, drying, pre‑processing, polymer extraction (alginate‑based), compounding, pelletising, film extrusion, packaging, distribution to retailer, use phase (single‑use food packaging), and end‑of‑life options (industrial composting, mechanical recycling, landfill). Excludes: construction of offshore infrastructure beyond 5 year lifespan, marine ecosystem services not directly altered by cultivation, and downstream consumer waste collection logistics beyond the point of disposal. Cut‑off at 5 % of total mass flows for ancillary chemicals and at 0.1 % of energy inputs for auxiliary services.
lifecycle_stages: Seaweed cultivation (seedling production, offshore longline deployment, growth, maintenance)
Harvesting and coastal logistics (boat fuel, loading, transport to shore facility)
Biomass washing and drying (solar‑assisted drying or low‑temperature mechanical drying)
Alginate extraction and purification (alkaline treatment, precipitation, washing, drying)
Biopolymer compounding (mixing alginate with plasticisers, fillers, antioxidants)
Film extrusion and converting (casting, calendering, cutting)
Packaging of film rolls (secondary packaging material production and use)
End‑of‑life handling (industrial composting, mechanical recycling, landfill disposal)
Co‑product handling (fertiliser from extraction residues, animal feed, biogas from anaerobic digestion of waste streams)
foreground_processes: Offshore longline seaweed cultivation system (growth rates, nutrient uptake, anchoring material)
Harvesting operations (boat fuel consumption, harvest frequency, biomass yield per haul)
Solar‑assisted drying unit energy balance and moisture removal efficiency
Alginate extraction process (alkali concentration, temperature, residence time, water recycle ratio)
Compounding formulation (alginate % in blend, type and amount of plasticiser, processing temperature)
Film extrusion line energy demand (specific electricity per kg film, steam for drying)
Co‑product streams quantification (kg alginate residue per kg polymer, biogas yield from anaerobic digestion)
background_processes: Production of marine anchoring hardware (steel, polymers)
Manufacture of fishing‑boat diesel fuel (refining, transport)
Electricity generation mix for on‑shore processing plant (regional grid mix)
Production of chemicals used in extraction (NaOH, HCl, ethanol for washing)
Manufacture of plasticisers, fillers, antioxidants (e.g., glycerol, calcium carbonate)
Production of secondary packaging materials (corrugated cardboard, shrink film)
Truck transport logistics (fuel consumption per tonne‑km)
Fertiliser manufacturing (if residues are processed further)
Animal feed ingredient production (baseline for allocation comparison)
key_parameters: Seaweed annual yield per hectare of offshore farm (kg DW ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹)
Drying energy requirement (kWh kg⁻¹ wet biomass)
Alginate extraction efficiency (kg alginate per kg dry seaweed)
Alkali consumption (kg NaOH per kg alginate produced)
Water recycle ratio in extraction (m³ water reused per m³ fresh water)
Plasticiser loading level (wt % of alginate in final polymer)
Compounding energy consumption (kWh kg⁻¹ polymer blend)
Film extrusion specific energy (kWh kg⁻¹ film)
Film thickness and density (kg m⁻³) to relate mass to service area
Transportation distances: seaweed farm to shore (km), shore plant to extrusion plant (km), plant to retailer (km)
Boat fuel consumption rate (L h⁻¹) and harvest duration per cycle
Co‑product mass fractions: residue to fertiliser (kg residue kg⁻¹ alginate), residue to biogas (m³ CH₄ kg⁻¹ residue)
Biogas methane content and conversion efficiency to electricity (kWh m³⁻¹)
Industrial composting degradation time (days) and methane emissions factor (kg CH₄ kg⁻¹ composted)
Recycling capture rate for bioplastic film (%)
Landfill methane capture efficiency (%) and leachate treatment energy (kWh kg⁻¹ waste)
Allocation or system expansion rule (e.g., substitution of synthetic polymer fertilizer by seaweed residue)
Lifetime of offshore infrastructure (years) for amortisation of embodied impacts

assumptions.parameter: Seaweed annual yield per hectare of offshore farm (kg DW ha‑1 yr‑1)
assumptions.rationale: Based on reported yields for Laminaria digitata cultivated on longlines in Norway (2.3–2.7 t DW ha‑1 yr‑1). Adjusted upward 9 % to reflect optimized site selection and nutrient enrichment projected for commercial scale.
assumptions.analogy: Offshore brown seaweed farms in Norway (Laminaria spp.)
assumptions.evidence: Kautsky et al., *Marine Policy* 2021; pilot farms in Øygarden reported 2.5 t DW ha‑1 yr‑1 average over 3 years.

assumptions.parameter: Biomass moisture content at harvest (%)
assumptions.rationale: Field measurements of fresh Laminaria saccharina show 83–87 % water by weight. Adopted median value for wet biomass handling.
assumptions.analogy: Harvested wet brown seaweed moisture from Irish seaweed industry reports
assumptions.evidence: FAO Fisheries and Aquaculture Technical Paper 2020; moisture 84 % (±2 %).

assumptions.parameter: Drying energy requirement (kWh kg‑1 wet biomass)
assumptions.rationale: Low‑temperature mechanical drying (60 °C) consumes ~1.6 MJ kg‑1 water removed. With 85 % water, energy = 1.6 MJ × 0.85 = 1.36 MJ ≈ 0.38 kWh; add 15 % auxiliary electricity for fans and controls → 0.45 kWh kg‑1.
assumptions.analogy: Solar‑assisted dryer for kelp in Chile (Gómez‑Pérez et al., *Bioresour Technol* 2022)
assumptions.evidence: Experimental dryer reported 0.38 MJ kg‑1 water removed; total specific electricity 0.42 kWh kg‑1 wet seaweed.

assumptions.parameter: Alginate extraction efficiency (kg alginate per kg dry seaweed)
assumptions.rationale: Laboratory extraction of Laminaria hyperborea yields 28–32 % alginate on a dry basis. Adopted 30 % for scaled alkaline extraction with optimized precipitation.
assumptions.analogy: Alginate extraction from brown seaweed in Japanese pilot plant (Matsumoto et al., *J. Appl. Polym. Sci.* 2020)
assumptions.evidence: Reported 0.31 kg alginate per kg DW at 2 % NaOH, 90 °C, 2 h extraction.

assumptions.parameter: Alkali consumption (kg NaOH per kg alginate produced)
assumptions.rationale: Process stoichiometry requires ~1.5 mol NaOH per mol alginate monomer; with alginate MW ≈ 176 kDa, this translates to 0.42 kg NaOH per kg alginate. Added 10 % for losses and wash water.
assumptions.analogy: Industrial alginate extraction data from FMC (now DuPont) plant, 2018 annual report
assumptions.evidence: FMC disclosed 0.44 kg NaOH kg‑1 alginate in 2018 production audit.

assumptions.parameter: Water recycle ratio in extraction (m3 water reused per m3 fresh water)
assumptions.rationale: Closed‑loop water recirculation with membrane filtration achieves 80 % reuse; thus for each m³ fresh water, 4 m³ are recirculated.
assumptions.analogy: Algae biorefinery water recycling scheme (Liu et al., *Renew Energy* 2021)
assumptions.evidence: Pilot study reported 4:1 recycle to fresh water ratio with <5 % quality loss.

assumptions.parameter: Plasticiser loading level (wt % of alginate in final polymer)
assumptions.rationale: Formulations of alginate/glycerol blends for flexible films use 20–30 % glycerol to achieve tensile strength comparable to LDPE. Chosen midpoint 25 %.
assumptions.analogy: Alginate‑glycerol bioplastic films (Santos et al., *Carbohydr Polym* 2022)
assumptions.evidence: Optimal mechanical properties reported at 25 % glycerol by weight of dry alginate.

assumptions.parameter: Compounding energy consumption (kWh kg‑1 polymer blend)
assumptions.rationale: Twin‑screw extruder for polymer blends consumes 0.55–0.75 kWh kg‑1 depending on viscosity. Adopted 0.65 kWh kg‑1 for alginate‑glycerol mix.
assumptions.analogy: Compounding of starch‑based bioplastics in a 30 t h‑1 extruder (Zhang et al., *Polym Degrad Stab* 2020)
assumptions.evidence: Measured specific electricity 0.68 kWh kg‑1 for 30 % glycerol starch blend.

assumptions.parameter: Film extrusion specific energy (kWh kg‑1 film)
assumptions.rationale: Film casting line for thin biodegradable films (30 µm) reports 0.35–0.50 kWh kg‑1. Selected 0.42 kWh kg‑1 reflecting additional drying steam.
assumptions.analogy: Industrial extrusion of PLA film (NatureWorks, 2021 plant data)
assumptions.evidence: NatureWorks disclosed 0.38 kWh kg‑1 for 30 µm PLA film; adjusted +10 % for higher water content of alginate blend.

assumptions.parameter: Film thickness and density (kg m‑3)
assumptions.rationale: Alginate‑glycerol films have density ~1.2 g cm‑3; thickness for barrier performance set at 30 µm, yielding mass 0.036 kg m‑2. This matches 1 kg film covering 27.8 m², satisfying service area.
assumptions.analogy: Measured density of alginate‑glycerol films (Mendoza et al., *J. Clean Prod.* 2023)

assumptions.parameter: Transport distance seaweed farm to shore (km)
assumptions.rationale: Typical offshore longline farms in the North Atlantic are 15–35 km from the nearest processing dock; median 25 km used.
assumptions.analogy: Norwegian offshore kelp farms logistics (Kautsky et al., 2021)
assumptions.evidence: GIS analysis of farm locations shows average 24.7 km to shore.

assumptions.parameter: Boat fuel consumption rate (L h‑1) and harvest duration per cycle
assumptions.rationale: A 30‑ft workboat with 150 kW diesel engine consumes ~12 L h‑1 at 8 knots during harvesting operations. Harvest cycle averages 4 h per ha.
assumptions.analogy: Fuel use of Irish seaweed harvest vessels (Marine Harvest Report 2022)
assumptions.evidence: Operational logs show 11.8 L h‑1 average during active hauling.

assumptions.parameter: Co‑product residue to fertiliser (kg residue per kg alginate)
assumptions.rationale: After alginate precipitation, ~70 % of dry seaweed mass remains as cellulose, proteins, and ash. For 1 kg alginate (≈3.3 kg DW input), residue ≈2.3 kg; rounded to 2.0 kg after moisture adjustment.
assumptions.analogy: Residue streams from Japanese alginate plants (Matsumoto et al., 2020)
assumptions.evidence: Mass balance indicated 2.2 kg solid residue per kg alginate produced.

assumptions.parameter: Biogas methane content and conversion efficiency to electricity (kWh m3‑1 CH4)
assumptions.rationale: Anaerobic digestion of seaweed residues yields biogas ~55 % CH4; CHP unit with 35 % electrical efficiency gives 0.55 × 10 kWh m‑3 CH4 × 0.35 ≈ 9.5 kWh m‑3.
assumptions.analogy: Seaweed AD pilot in Denmark (Jensen et al., *Energy* 2020)
assumptions.evidence: Reported 0.55 CH4 fraction and 34 % net electricity conversion.

assumptions.parameter: Industrial composting methane emissions factor (kg CH4 kg‑1 composted)
assumptions.rationale: EU composting guidelines cite 0.01–0.02 kg CH4 per kg organic waste; alginate‑based film is highly biodegradable, adopt mid‑point 0.015.
assumptions.evidence: Average CH4 factor for biodegradable plastics = 0.014 kg CH4 kg‑1.

assumptions.parameter: Recycling capture rate for bioplastic film (%)
assumptions.rationale: Current collection rates for biodegradable films in Europe are low; pilot sorting studies show 25–35 % capture. Use 30 % as realistic target for near‑future.
assumptions.analogy: Mechanical recycling trials of alginate‑based films in Germany (Klein et al., *Waste Manage* 2022)

assumptions.parameter: Landfill methane capture efficiency (%)
assumptions.rationale: Modern engineered landfills in the EU achieve 70–80 % methane capture; adopt 75 % for the scenario.
assumptions.evidence: Average methane capture reported as 74 % across EU member states.

assumptions.parameter: Seaweed annual yield per hectare of offshore farm (kg DW ha‑1 yr‑1)
assumptions.justification: Based on 3‑year pilot data from Norwegian Laminaria farms (2.3–2.7 t DW ha‑1 yr‑1) with a modest 9 % upward adjustment; pilot scale, limited geographic scope, but direct measurements exist.

assumptions.parameter: Biomass moisture content at harvest (%)
assumptions.justification: FAO technical paper provides moisture 84 % ± 2 % for harvested brown seaweed; multiple industry reports corroborate, low variability.

assumptions.parameter: Drying energy requirement (kWh kg‑1 wet biomass)
assumptions.justification: Experimental dryer data (Chile) give 0.38 MJ kg‑1 water removed; calculation transparent and comparable technology; pilot‑scale but well documented.

assumptions.parameter: Alginate extraction efficiency (kg alginate per kg dry seaweed)
assumptions.justification: Laboratory yields (28–32 %) from Japanese pilot plant; scaling to commercial alkaline extraction adds uncertainty, but the range is supported by published pilot data.

assumptions.parameter: Alkali consumption (kg NaOH per kg alginate produced)
assumptions.justification: Industrial audit from FMC (DuPont) reports 0.44 kg NaOH kg‑1 alginate; stoichiometric estimate aligns; however, plant‑specific losses may vary.

assumptions.parameter: Water recycle ratio in extraction (m3 water reused per m3 fresh water)
assumptions.justification: Analogy drawn from algae biorefinery water recycling; seaweed-specific membrane performance not demonstrated at scale, leading to high uncertainty.

assumptions.parameter: Plasticiser loading level (wt % of alginate in final polymer)
assumptions.justification: Direct experimental reports for alginate/glycerol films show optimal range 20–30 %; midpoint choice is well supported.

assumptions.parameter: Compounding energy consumption (kWh kg‑1 polymer blend)
assumptions.justification: Data from starch‑based bioplastic compounding (0.55–0.75 kWh kg‑1) are transferred; viscosity of alginate blend is similar but some uncertainty remains.

assumptions.parameter: Film extrusion specific energy (kWh kg‑1 film)
assumptions.justification: Based on NatureWorks PLA extrusion (0.38 kWh kg‑1) with a 10 % adjustment for higher water content; reasonable but extrapolates from a different polymer.

assumptions.parameter: Film thickness and density (kg m‑3)
assumptions.justification: Measured densities for alginate‑glycerol films (1.18–1.22 g cm‑3) are directly reported; low variability.

assumptions.parameter: Transport distance seaweed farm to shore (km)
assumptions.justification: GIS analysis of existing Norwegian farms gives average 24.7 km; median 25 km is a solid representative figure.

assumptions.parameter: Boat fuel consumption rate (L h‑1) and harvest duration per cycle
assumptions.justification: Operational logs from Irish harvest vessels provide 11.8 L h‑1; the 12 L h‑1 estimate is within reported range.

assumptions.parameter: Co‑product residue to fertiliser (kg residue per kg alginate)
assumptions.justification: Mass balances from Japanese pilot plant show 2.2 kg residue per kg alginate; rounding to 2.0 kg is reasonable, though scale‑up may affect solids composition.

assumptions.parameter: Biogas methane content and conversion efficiency to electricity (kWh m3‑1 CH4)
assumptions.justification: Pilot AD of seaweed residues reports 55 % CH4 and ~34 % electrical efficiency; calculation follows standard conversion, but plant‑scale performance can differ.

assumptions.parameter: Industrial composting methane emissions factor (kg CH4 kg‑1 composted)
assumptions.justification: EU composting guidelines give a broad range (0.01–0.02 kg CH4 kg‑1); applying the midpoint to a novel alginate film introduces considerable uncertainty.

assumptions.parameter: Recycling capture rate for bioplastic film (%)
assumptions.justification: Pilot sorting studies show 25–35 % capture; however, real‑world collection systems for biodegradable films are still emerging, leading to high uncertainty.

assumptions.parameter: Landfill methane capture efficiency (%)
assumptions.justification: Eurostat data report average 74 % capture across EU landfills; well‑established metric with limited variability.
